verses.1: Al-Mizan reports a company of jinn hearing a wonderful recitation that guides to rectitude, believing it, and vowing never to associate partners with their Lord.
verses.2: Al-Mizan reports a company of jinn hearing a wonderful recitation that guides to rectitude, believing it, and vowing never to associate partners with their Lord.
verses.3: Al-Mizan says their exalted Lord has neither spouse nor son.
verses.4: Al-Mizan says a foolish one among them uttered atrocious lies about Allah.
verses.5: Al-Mizan records their former belief that neither humans nor jinn would lie about Allah.
verses.6: Al-Mizan says humans sought protection from jinn, thereby adding only to their rebellion.
verses.7: Al-Mizan says they thought Allah would raise no one.
verses.8: Al-Mizan says they found heaven filled with strong guards and meteors.
verses.9: Al-Mizan says the jinn once eavesdropped there, but any listener now meets a waiting flame.
verses.10: Al-Mizan records the jinn’s uncertainty whether earth’s people face evil or their Lord’s guidance.
verses.11: Al-Mizan says some jinn are righteous, others otherwise, in diverse groups.
verses.12: Al-Mizan says they know no flight or earthbound act can thwart Allah.
verses.13: Al-Mizan says that, on hearing the guidance, they believed; whoever believes in his Lord fears neither loss nor oppression.
verses.14: Al-Mizan distinguishes jinn who submit to Allah and pursue rectitude from those who are perverse.
verses.15: Al-Mizan says the perverse will be firewood for hell.
verses.16: Al-Mizan identifies this Meccan, 28-verse sūrah as the story of jinn who heard the Qur’an, believed, and embraced its precepts; it thereby affirms the Prophet’s mission, God’s Lordly oneness, and the hereafter. God commands the Prophet to report the revelation: a nafar of jinn heard the Qur’an and described it as ʿajab, extraordinary in form and content despite being brought by an unlettered man. Al-rushd is the truth and real happiness reached through its theoretical and practical teachings, opposite ghayy. Their immediate faith confirms the Qur’an and, with it, God’s Lordship and an unqualified refusal to associate partners with Him. Nafar commonly denotes three to nine, though some extend it to forty. The commentary holds that jinn are beyond human sensory perception but are Qur’an-affirmed creatures: created before human beings from fire, mortal and resurrected, sexed and procreating, intelligent and free, able to perform arduous tasks, and religiously obligated, so they include believers and disbelievers, pious and impious. It notes their work for Solomon and identifies Iblīs, with descendants and followers, as one of them. For the declaration that God has neither spouse nor son, jadd can mean either divine greatness or resources, and either sense establishes His freedom from both. The repeated particle annahu in verses (72:3) through (72:14) has fatḥah and kasrah readings; innahu is preferred because the verses continue the jinn’s direct speech. Joining it to the object of the jinn’s belief, tying it to that object’s grammatical position, or supplying an omitted bāʾ are proposed but do not account for the subsequent clauses. The only acceptable fatḥah explanation supplies an implicit clause appropriate to each utterance. Treating every occurrence as a repeat of “It is revealed unto me” is rejected as disrupting the report and producing either redundancy or incomplete speech. Safah is frivolity born of folly and shaṭaṭ speech far from truth. The “foolish one” denotes the earlier polytheists among the jinn, not Iblīs: the plural wording and “used to utter” describe an ongoing practice up to revelation. The jinn had trusted claims from humans and jinn that God had a wife and children, followed that path into polytheism, and only the Qur’an unveiled the truth; they therefore denounce polytheists of both kinds. Al-Mizan glosses ʿawdh as seeking refuge and rahaq as being forcefully overtaken, with sin, rebellion, fear, evil, humiliation, and weakness as related senses. It reports an Arab desert custom of seeking a jinn chief’s protection; Muqātil attributes its beginning to a Yemeni tribe, then Banū Ḥanīfah, before its spread among the Arabs. Seeking jinn through divination is another possibility, and the reading that people sought other people’s protection from jinn reduces to the same idea. The pronouns may mean that humans increased the jinn’s rebellion, or that jinn increased humans’ rahaq, whether sin and rebellion or humiliation and fear. In verse (72:7), “they” are the humans just mentioned, and the jinn address their own fellows. “Raise” means appointing a messenger, not resurrecting the dead, as the context confirms; the claim that these verses are a divine parenthesis rather than jinn speech is rejected because it breaks their continuous discourse. Lams means approaching heaven by rising, while ḥaras are strong guards whose meteors prevent eavesdropping. The new event accompanying the Qur’an’s revelation and the Prophet’s mission is the jinn’s exclusion from heavenly news. The point is not whether there had previously been some guards, meteors, or empty places—this cannot be proved from the verse—but that the jinn were now repelled from all eavesdropping places. The novelty lies in meteors’ guarding function against them, not meteors’ mere existence. Rushd and rashad oppose ghayy, and the indefinite rashadan denotes a particular guidance. The jinn’s uncertainty about the earthly consequence of their exclusion contrasts evil with guidance, the latter implying divine grace and happiness. Their active attribution of guidance to God and passive expression of evil show courtesy; evil is not willed for someone except through that person’s qualifying misdeeds. In verse (72:11), dūna means “other,” not “near,” and “righteous” apparently means a natural disposition in dealings, not religious righteousness. Their multifarious ways may mean that they are in such groups, possess them through an omitted term, or are metaphorically like diverging paths. Their ẓann is certain knowledge that no corruption on earth can thwart God’s will, because it remains within His causal system, and flight offers no escape if He pursues them. The interpretation that contrasts earth with an unstated heaven is rejected. The guidance they heard is the Qur’an; bakhs is unjust deficiency and rahaq hardship overtaking one. The faʾ shows why they believed without hesitation: faith in one’s Lord entails neither lost good nor wrongful hardship. Islām here is taslīm, surrender to the divine command; the muslimūn obey it and seek the truth, whereas the qāsiṭūn incline from truth to falsehood. Majmaʿ al-bayān distinguishes qāsiṭ, one who turns from truth, from muqsiṭ, one who turns toward it. The perverse become firewood because their very selves and souls burn in hell; exegetes differ whether this ending remains the jinn’s speech or becomes God’s address to the Prophet. Finally, an is the unstressed form of anna and links the conditional to the opening report. The path is submission with its requirements, including faith in God and His communications. Ghadaq means profuse abundance; abundant water may metaphorically mean material expansion, as the following test indicates. Thus jinn and humans who remain steadfast receive abundant sustenance as a test of their material well-being.
verses.17: Al-Mizan explains ṣaʿadan as a punishment that rises and prevails over its victim, though some interpret it as excruciating torment. Turning from God’s remembrance is stated as the cause of entering hell, while being inseparable from failure to remain steadfast on the path. The shift from “We” to “his Lord” grounds this punishment in divine Lordship and indicates the agency at work in it.
verses.18: Places of worship belong to Allah; invoke none alongside Him.
verses.19: When Allah’s servant prayed, they nearly crowded round him.
verses.20: He says he prays only to his Lord and ascribes no partner to Him.
verses.21: I cannot harm or guide you.
verses.22: Al-Mizan says the Prophet can find neither protection nor refuge from Allah; his duty is only to transmit Allah’s messages, and disobedience to Allah and His Messenger brings everlasting hellfire.
verses.23: Al-Mizan says the Prophet can find neither protection nor refuge from Allah; his duty is only to transmit Allah’s messages, and disobedience to Allah and His Messenger brings everlasting hellfire.
verses.24: Al-Mizan says that when they see the promise, they will know who has weaker support and fewer numbers.
verses.25: Al-Mizan says the Prophet does not know whether the promise is near or has a fixed term.
verses.26: Al-Mizan presents these verses as the conclusion to the jinn narrative: they confirm prophethood, tawḥīd, resurrection, and the preservation of God’s message. It reads duʿāʾ in (72:18) as ʿibādah, as (40:60) shows, so that God’s exclusive ownership of the masājid proves that none may be worshipped with Him. The plural rules out restricting masājid to the Kaʿbah or one or two mosques; the ḥaram reading is unwarranted; the report that earth is a prayer-place only permits Muslims to pray anywhere; and ritual prayer has no supporting evidence. On the narration from Imam al-Jawād, also reported from Saʿīd b. Jubayr, al-Farrāʾ, and al-Zajjāj, it prefers the seven limbs of prostration, legally assigned to God alone; duʿāʾ therefore means prostration specifically, or prayer insofar as it includes prostration. At (72:19), libad means a dense group and “the servant of Allah” is the Prophet: the contextual referent of “they” is the polytheists who mocked and shouted over his prayer and recitation, not jinn or believers, whose proposed readings do not fit what follows. His declaration in (72:20) answers their suspicion of a plot against idols or worldly scheme: he worships his Lord alone. In (72:21) he denies independent power to harm or benefit—or to bring rashad, guidance—and must simply convey God’s command; one reported lexical reading makes ḍarr the result of ghayy, the opposite of rashad. Al-Mizan explains ijārah as protective shelter and multaḥad as a place of turning aside for safety. The exception in (72:23) attaches to having no refuge: whether balāgh min Allah contains an ellipsis or min is read as ʿan, the Prophet’s sole course is to communicate God’s names, attributes, and messages concerning religious duties. Making the exception qualify (72:21) instead would break the verse’s harmony. The Messenger is paired with God because he only communicates His message, and the threatened disobedience is rejection of tawḥīd, or of tawḥīd and the religion’s roots and branches, not every ordinary sin; the verse therefore does not prove that all sinners remain eternally in hell. At (72:24), “until” presupposes the polytheists’ continuing contempt for the Prophet’s weak and few supporters, which will end when they see the promised hellfire; (72:25) answers their implied question about its time, while amad means an endpoint. Al-Mizan takes “Knower of the unseen” in (72:26) to establish that all unseen knowledge belongs to God intrinsically and exclusively. Iẓhār with ʿalā is authorization to overcome or know something, and the wording yields a total, not merely partial, negation: no one knows any of His unseen independently. The exception for a messenger pleasing to God means that God may teach His messengers whatever portion of it He wills. This reconciles the exclusivist texts (6:59), (11:123), (16:77), and (27:65): God knows bil-aṣālah, intrinsically and primarily, while others know bil-tabaʿ, secondarily through His teaching, as acts of taking souls are primarily God’s though also attributed to the angels (39:42), (32:11), and (6:61). The sentinels in (72:27) are guardian angels stationed along both routes of revelation—between God and the messenger and between the messenger and the people—to prevent satanic addition or loss. “So that He may ascertain” is God’s knowledge in action, the actual fulfillment of the messages’ intact communication, not new information for Him. Al-Mizan rejects readings that make the guards surround the unseen itself, identify the referent as Gabriel, make the messenger verify angels’ delivery, make him learn that predecessors conveyed, or make deniers learn it: the grammar and purpose concern messengers communicating to their people, and guards protect rather than transmit. God’s encompassing knowledge of what is with the messengers completes preservation in three stages: revelation’s descent to the messenger, its retention in his soul, and its delivery to the people. From this Al-Mizan infers that messengers are immune from error in receiving, retaining, and conveying revelation, and, because deeds also communicate religion, from sin and neglected duty; prophets share this infallibility because nubuwwah and risālah both involve revelation. The verses’ rule concerns people living in this world. If rasūl is specific, prophets are further exceptions because they receive revelation (4:163); if general, it already includes nabī, as in (22:52) and (7:94). It also identifies Qur’anic imāms, described by patience and certainty (32:24) and removal of the veil ((6:75); (102:5-6)), as another exception; the dead and angels are not exceptions because their respective worlds make those realities visible to them. Finally, the exception extends to unseen matters needed for a messenger’s mission—doctrines, laws, narratives, wisdom, admonition, miracles, promises, threats, and predictions—such as Ṣāliḥ’s three-day warning (11:65) and Jesus’ knowledge of what people ate and stored (3:49).
